en: The Discourse on the Eight Recollections Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhi Yao of the Western Regions during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Ximucheng beneath the Qushi tree. The Venerable...
Aniruddha, while sitting in meditation within that empty marsh, reflected and said:
"The Dharma of the Path consists in few desires; many desires are not the Path.
The Dharma of the Path consists in contentment; insatiability is not the Path."
The Way and Dharma lie in seclusion; delighting in crowds is not the Way.
The Way and Dharma require diligence; indolence is not the Way.
The Way and Dharma require the disciplining of the mind; dissipation is not the Way.
"The dharmas of the Path consist in the stabilization of the mind; manifold thoughts are not the Path.
The dharmas of the Path consist in wisdom; ignorance and darkness are not the Path.
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts in advance with his noble mind, flew before them in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm and praised them, saying:
“Excellent, excellent,
Aniruddha! That which you contemplate is the contemplation of a Mahāsattva.”
Listen as I speak to you, Great Being, regarding the eight recollections; contemplate them well and practice them.
You should train in the four dhyānas, restraining the mind and observing the dharmas without ceasing; thus you will surely attain great benefit and not fail in your aspirations.
What are the four dhyānas?
Merely abandoning desires, evils, and unwholesome states, with a mind filled with joy, constitutes the practice of the first dhyāna.
By relinquishing evil thoughts and concentrating the mind on a single object, no longer relying on joy, one attains the practice of the second dhyāna.
Abiding in joy, one contemplates and perceives pleasure and pain in accordance with the Dharma; this constitutes the practice of the third dhyāna.
Furthermore, abandoning both pleasure and pain, and severing both sorrow and joy, one dwells in purity; this constitutes the practice of the fourth dhyāna.
Having trained in this manner, one thereafter contemplates and practices the eight thoughts of a great person (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*).
Taking the four dhyānas as the method for restraining the mind, one gains clear insight into practice, attains swift progress toward the desired goal, and no longer halts midway.

Furthermore, as for the meaning of "having few desires": it is like a king who has a border official in charge of many chests filled with colorful garments, yet that official himself delights in wearing coarse and tattered clothes. One who has few desires and is content, who practices diligence in seclusion, who restrains the mind and fixes the will, who uses wisdom to leave the household life, and who does not act with frivolity or arrogance, remaining without error—such a person will surely bring peace and security to others and reach the gate of Nirvana.

These are the eight recollections of a great man; one should simply use the four dhyānas to restrain the mind and contemplate the Dharma. The meaning of this is like a king who has frontier ministers overseeing the kitchen masters to harmonize the five flavors, while you yourself take pleasure in begging for food, merely seeking to sustain the body without seeking mental joy.

The meaning of this is as follows: it is like a king who possesses a pleasure pavilion for excursions, yet you yourself delight in dwelling in seclusion among the mountains, marshes, and trees, practicing diligence and having no desire for the world.

The meaning is also like a king who has a border official in charge of various excellent medicines, including curd, clarified butter, *sarpis*, and rock honey, yet you yourself delight in taking those intended for the sick, which serve merely to temporarily relieve distress through the small urine.

"By practicing the eight recollections, contemplating the four dhyānas, being diligent without fail, and keeping the mind from straying, one will surely attain peace and security and reach the gate of Nirvāṇa.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha returned to Śrāvastī and addressed his disciples:
"The Way requires few desires; do not harbor many desires."
The Way requires contentment, with no accumulation of surplus;
the Way requires seclusion, with no delight in crowds;
the Way requires diligence, with no falling into indolence.
The Way requires that you restrain the mind and not be negligent;
the Way requires that you concentrate the intent and not harbor distracted thoughts;
the Way requires that you possess wisdom and not remain in ignorant darkness.
“Monks, it is a blessing to have few desires; that is, one should personally have few desires oneself, yet not cause others to know that one has few desires—one should follow this principle.

Monks, it is to be content with what one has; that is, regarding the alms bowl, Dharma robes, bedding, and medicine for illness, one should be satisfied with what is obtained and stop there, not hoarding or accumulating leftovers—one should follow this principle.”
"A bhikṣu’s seclusion means avoiding human society, not entering assemblies, and dwelling far away among mountains, marshes, crags, and trees.
If members of the fourfold assembly, such as kings or high ministers, come to seek the Way, he preaches to them for the sake of purity so that they may depart quickly."

For example, it is like a poor man who has incurred a debt to a person of noble lineage; when dragged and pulled by his creditor, he wishes to escape and does not take pleasure in remaining, seeking instead to hide away and flee far off—it is right that he should act according to this principle.

So too, a bhikṣu is diligent, meaning he severs what is contrary to the Dharma and zealously practices the path of the sūtras without ever becoming weary. Throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, whether walking, sitting, or lying down, he remains constantly awake and mindful, purifying his thoughts to eliminate the five hindrances—it is right that he should act according to this principle.

“A bhikṣu should restrain the mind, abandon desires and unwholesome states, and sit with focused attention to contemplate, thereby severing both suffering and pleasure; he shall attain the practice of the four dhyānas, for this is the proper course.”

"A bhikṣu’s concentrated mind means being constantly single-minded, contemplating the body, contemplating the mind, and contemplating phenomena; not engaging in worldly conduct, he collects his mindfulness and proceeds toward the Path, abandoning deluded and afflictive thoughts—this is what the principle requires."
“The wisdom of a bhikṣu consists in knowing the Four Noble Truths:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
What is the truth of suffering?”

The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one desires, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.

"Suffering of birth" refers to a person following their karma to fall [into a womb], receiving the formation of the embryo, emerging with physical form manifest, and the growth of the sense faculties and limbs.

"Suffering of old age" refers to a person whose faculties have matured and whose form has changed: hair turns white, teeth fall out, tendons loosen, skin wrinkles, and one walks with a stoop, leaning on a staff.
"Sickness" refers to that which results from a person's unwholesome deeds: such as carbuncles, abscesses, sores, pus, epilepsy, chronic illnesses, and more than a hundred other varieties.
"Death" refers to the passing away of life and the disintegration of the physical form, where warmth is extinguished, breath ceases, and the soul departs.
All these are suffering.
What is the Truth of Origination?

It refers to the arising of affectionate attachment through the mind’s delight and joy in sensual passion; with the will fixed on greed and desire, it causes further outflows to arise, so that all conditioned formations flourish and one becomes bound by clinging to them.

What is called "craving" (tṛṣṇā) refers to the eye craving forms, the ear craving sounds, the nose craving fragrances, the tongue craving tastes, the body craving tactile sensations, and the mind craving its desires;

merely observing that what is constantly pleasant lies within one's reach, one takes it as a benefit and calls out, "This is mine. Through this attachment, one binds oneself. Consequently, craving for the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—intensifies; seeing them as permanent and delighting in them, one says, "This is mine," and through this attachment, one binds oneself.
What is called "form" (rūpa) refers to the physical manifestations produced by the transformation of the vital spirits' reception of the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind;

through attachment to these, one causes the eye-consciousness to perceive forms, the ear-consciousness to perceive sounds, the nose-consciousness to perceive fragrances, the tongue-consciousness to perceive tastes, the body-consciousness to perceive tactile sensations, and the mind-consciousness to become attached to mental phenomena—this clinging is identified as the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).
What is the truth of cessation?

It is non-appropriation and non-entry; it is the exhaustion of craving without remainder, the complete liberation from bondage and attachment, because for one who sees with wisdom, nothing further exists.
Ordinary people see nothing and are attached to the five aggregates;

when their calculations are exhausted and the bonds of craving are completely severed, they have already abandoned [the world] through the vision of wisdom as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—this is the Truth of Cessation.
What is the Truth of the Path?
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
What is right view?
Right view is twofold:
there is the mundane and there is the supramundane.

To know that benevolence and righteousness exist; to know that parents exist; to know that śramaṇas and brahmins exist; to know that true persons who have attained the Way exist; to know that this world and the next world exist; and to know that there are good and evil, as well as retribution for sins and blessings—proving these through one's own conduct from this life to the next—this is called right view regarding the world.
Having understood the Four Truths—
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— and having attained the wisdom and vision that they are empty, pure, and not-self, this constitutes right view regarding the Path.
Right thought also has two aspects:
To contemplate learning, to contemplate harmony and respect, to contemplate caution and vigilance, and to contemplate non-harming—these are called right thoughts pertaining to the world.
To contemplate renunciation, to contemplate patience and silence, and to contemplate the extinction of craving and the ending of attachment—these are called right thoughts pertaining to the Path.
Right speech also has two aspects:
not engaging in double-tongued speech, not using harsh abuse, not speaking falsehoods, and not indulging in frivolous chatter—this is mundane right speech;

to be free from these four verbal transgressions, to recite and expound the words of the Way, and to ensure that no further mental constructions arise, leaving nothing remaining—this is the right speech of the Way.
Right practice also has two aspects:
practicing good with the body, speaking good with the mouth, and thinking good with the mind—this is mundane right practice;
exerting oneself with body and speech while the mind contemplates emptiness and purity, thereby dissolving and extinguishing all attachments—this is the right practice of the Path.
Right governance also has two aspects:
refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; not being conceited; cultivating virtue and maintaining self-restraint—this is called mundane right governance.
Departing from the three evils of the body, severing the accumulation of suffering, extinguishing craving, and seeking liberation—this is called the right governance of the Path.
Right livelihood also has two aspects:
seeking wealth through proper means without coveting gain or resorting to deceit toward others is mundane right livelihood;
to distance oneself from wrong occupations, abandon worldly divination and portents, and not violate the prohibitions of the Path is the right livelihood of the Path.
Right intention also has two aspects:
being without envy, without anger, and not serving what is heterodox—this is right intention of the world;
being free from the three evils of the mind, practicing the four bases of mindfulness, and being pure and unconditioned—this is right intention of the Path.
Right Concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) also has two types:
when the nature of the body is pure and harmonious, one maintains goodness with stability, and the mind is not crooked or deviant—this is mundane right concentration;

when one attains the four *dhyānas*, contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and perceives the source of *nirvāṇa*—this is the right concentration of the Path, which constitutes the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

A bhikṣu renounces the household life and abandons affection and love; he dwells in tranquility, contemplating the Way without longing or attachment. His mind does not follow desire; it is pure and free from hindrance. This is the Dharma of the Way, and its meaning should be followed accordingly.

When the venerable Anuruddha heard the Buddha preach this sutra, his mind was opened and guided; he practiced it for three months, exhausted the outflows (*āsrava*), attained liberation of mind, and having realized the three purifications as his own testimony, he knew within himself that he had become an Arhat. He then spoke these verses:
"One who desires without satiety, Who delights in crowds and indulges the mind— Such conduct leads to suffering, For practicing evil brings much attachment."
Having few desires and knowing the path of practice, possessing a sense of shame and not being self-conceited—
this Dharma leads to purity, distancing one from evil and bringing about transcendence in the world.
With the mind set on the Path, one does not crave life, nor does one delight in death or parting.
By means of the concentration that is like space, all sufferings await their time [to end].
Having received the Teacher’s instructions, I maintain my practice and abandon desire and evil;
having cast off the afflictions of the body, I have attained benefit and proceeded toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Having personally attained the three stages of mastery, And having already uprooted the source of affection and craving,
At the village of Vaiśālī, in the Bamboo Grove, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Ānanda-aṣṭānusmṛti-sūtra*.
